TEXAS. From an American Paper. The Batavia Spirit of the Times , contains an interesting letter from .Mr. Folett, formerly of Batuvia, and now a citizen of Texas þÿ We extract the concluding paragraphs: þÿ " The moral condition of the couutry, is wretched beyond comparison. No spire lifts its head to heaven, indicating that here the living God is worshipped ; no altar round which the ' poor in spirit' may assemble and offer up prayer to Him ' who rideth upon the whirlwind and directs the storm.' Perhaps there never was a country in which profanity and irreligion so universally prevailed as in this. It is none of your modern northern profanity, but the real double and twisted guarded and noted southern article, which is entirely different from any thing 1 ever saw or heard. Here they desecrate the name of their Maker, with as much ease and freedom as a northern man pursues his ordinary avocations of life. No matter whether it is in the company of ladies or gentlemen, it is all the same. Those at the north, who are particularly solicitous for the conversion of the heathen, and to send out missionaries for that purpose, would do well to direct their attention to this delightful but most certainly benighted land " Persons coming (o this country, expecting to find a perfect climate, will meet with disappointment. 1 hesitate not to say that I have suffered as much from the cold, during the past winter, as ever J did at the north. þÿ 1 his however, does not arise altogether from

the severity of the weather ; it is owing more to the slight preparations made to encounter it. þÿ The houses here, generally, are so open, that at the north we should not think of wintering a dumb beast in them. The weather is now warm and pleasant. Every thing is putting 011 the agreeable and enlivening appearance of spring. " 1 he Indians are the chief source of discontent to the inhabitants at the present lime. It is but a few days since, that a family by the name of Goacher, consisting of husband, wife, and seven children, were murdered bv them, Colonel Barnes is now fitting out an expedition to proceed into the Indian country. His chief object is to conclude a treaty with the Cama aches. It will be a desirable trip to be made, and bad I not been so long absent from home, I would join the expedition. A novel method of treating prisoners of war i3 practised in this country. Thev are parcelled out to those who will clothe and feed them, and made to perform the duty of þÿslaves and are treated as such They are generally quiet and inoffensive, and perform their task without complaint. Yours, &.c. J.\»

MAN. It has been often made a subject of dispute þÿ What is the distinguishing characteristic of man' And the answer may, perhaps, be given, that he is the only animal that dt 'esses. He is the only being who is coxcomb enough rot to go out of the world naked as he came into it ; that is ashamed of what he really is, and proud of what he is not ; and that tries to passofl'an artificial disguise as himself. We may safely extend the old maxim, and say that it is the tailor that makes both the

It is not his body alone that lie tampers with, and metamorphoses so successfully ; he tricks out his niind and soul in borrowed finery, and in tin: admired costume of gravity and imposture It lie has a desire to commit a base or cruel ae.tion without remorse and with the applause ol the spectators, he has only to throw th cloak of religion over it, and invoke Heaven to set its seal on a massacre or a robbery. At one time dirt, at another indecency, at another rapine, at a fourth rancorous malignity, is decked out and accredited

Again, we dress up our enemies in nicknames, and they march to the stake as assuredly as in sau lienilos. rl ho words Heretic or Papist, Jew or Infidel, labelled on those who differ from us, stand us in lieu of sense or decency. If a man be mean, he sets up for economy ; if selfish, he pretends to be prudent ; if harsh, firm ; and so on. What enormities, w hat follies are not undertaken for the love of glory ? glory of God Strange, that a reptile should þÿ and the worst of all, are said to be for the ' wish to be thought an angel ; or that he should not be content to writhe and grovel in his native earth, without aspiring to the skies ! It is front the love of dress and finery. lie is the chimney-sweeper on May-day all die year round: the soot peeps through the rags and tinsel, and all the flowers ol sentiment ! The mean.ng of all which is, that man is the only hypociite in the creation ; or that lie is composed of two natures, the ideal and the physical, the one of which lie is always trying to keep a secret from the other. He is the Centaur not fabulous þÿ « X J- r - Lady's Look. u VVe live to Learn " It is of little consequence what people learn, unless they learn discretion. Here is a world which has been running on almost six thousand years. Generation succeeding generation, and each professing to be wiser than that which preceded it þÿ and yet after

all, how small is the progress of the human mind in the essential principles of true wisdom. Age after age has recorded the history of its follies for the study of posterity, but tlie lessons have been successively read and uniformly forgotten. How few read the history of tlio past with a view to profit by the examples it contains of human weakness and human crime. 1 ho story of misfortunes awaken a temporary þÿinterest but how few gentleman and the man. Fine feathers make \ to avoid than. The narrative of sufferings j I search carefully into their causes with a view

wr.w «i produces its momentary effect upon the heart, who ol us traces up the link of the clmin which connects them with their parent follies, and profit by the study. Whoever has read the works and history of Xenophen, has admired more the discretion with which his genius and fancy invested the great Cyrus, than the wisdom which ho displayed himself. The son of Philip of Macedon, though trained in the school of the ablest politician -and soldier of the age, was himself little better than an adventurous madman. The boasted wisdom of the Athenians drivelled down into effeminacy and terminated in barbarism. And Rome bad scarcely learned to rule the world before she ceased to rule herself. Demosthenes covered himself with glory in the forum, and with disgrace in the field. Cicero with his eloquence turned Ceaser from his purpose, and fell a victim at last to irresolution and weakness. Saliust delighted the world with his splendid cnconiums upon vir. toe, and wrote them in the Sallustine palace which he had built and decorated with the fruits ol his own rapine and injustice. And the lives of the Roman Emperors downwards from the Augustan age, affords but one continued commentary upon the misei able lollies of human greatness. How little modern ages have profited by past lessons might easily be shown, How little men learn from the experience of others, is seen every day. " With all thy getting, get understanding," is the wisest of rccepts, and the least heeded by mankind. Now all this is the result of natural imbe-

cility ; no, most men reason well. The difficulty is, that it is not permitted to rule þÿ it is one branch of the government. The passions divide the empire with reason þÿ and man is governed by which ever power has the ascendancy for the time It is amusing and instructive, sometimes, to listen to the colloquies between the rivai parlies. I see a youth setting under yonder tree his brow upon his hand, lie is pondering the path of his future lilo þÿ Reason is pointing him to the long, pleasant and quiet vnilev of unambitious life þÿ recommends industry, frugality and temperance ; urges that in that path there are comparitively hut few trial's and þÿtemptations that it is free from the disquietude and mischances attendant upon every other þÿcourse that he may spend his days in peace and contentment, il he but listens 10 her þÿcounsels enjoying all the real sweets of life, he will experience hut few of its vicissitudes. He listens and his judgment is convinced. But then ambition raises her voice and she is an elegant dcclaimcr. (She points him to a path ol enterprise, and talks of wealth and glory, and renown þÿ tells him of the pleasure of the world þÿ interests him with isolated examples of success, until he feels himself ashamed of his humble counsellor, and gives himself away to ambition. It is not that reason is absent, hut that the passions of heart are more powerful. 'We live to learn;" yet what shall wc learn with such counsellors, hut "to know the right and yet the wrong pursue."

' There's danger in the mines, old man,' 1 asked of an age miner, who, with his arms bent, leaned against the side of the immense Vault absorbed in meditation þÿ ' it must be a fearful life 1 The old man looked at me with a steadfast but somewhat vacant stare, and then in half broken sentence he uttered " Danger ; where is there not 011 the earth, or beneath it, in the mountain or in the valley on the ocean or in the quiet of nature's most hidden spot þÿ where is there not danger ? where has death not left some token of his presence ?" ' True,' I replied, ' but the vicissitudes of life are various; the sailor seeks bis living on the waters, and he knows each moment that they may cngulph him; the hunter seeks death in the wild woods ; and the soldier in the battle (iold ; and the miner knows not but the spot where he now stands to-morrow may be tiis tomb.' ' It is so, indeed,' replied the old man, ' we find death in the means we seek to perpetuate life ; 'tis a strange riddle ; who shall solve it V ' Have you long followed this occupation V I asked, somewhat struck witli the old man's manner. 'From a hoy; I drew mv first breath in the mines, I shall yield it up in their gloom.' ' You have seen some of the vicissitudes,' said 1, to which you have just now alluded ' ' 'Yes,' he replied, with a faltering voice ' I have. There was a time that three tall hoys looked up to me and called me father. They were sturdy striplings ! Now it seems hut yesterday they stood before me so proud

in their strength and I tilled too with a lather's vanity. But the Lord chasteneth the proud heart. Where are they now? I raw the youngest, he was the dearest of the flock, his mother's spirit seemed to have settled on him, crushed at my feet a bleeding mass. þÿ We were together ; so near that his hot blood sprung up into my face Molten lead had been less lasting than those fearful drops. þÿ One moment and his light laugh was in my ears : the next, and the larger mass ran e ; there was no cry ; no look of terror ; hut the transaction to eternity was as the lightning's flash ; arid my poor boy lay crushed beneath the fearful load. It was an awful moment ; but time that ehangeth all things brought relief ; and 1 had still two sons. But my cup of affliction was not yet full. They too w ere taken from me, side by side they died, not as their brother; hut the fire damp caught their breath, and left them scorched and lifeless. þÿ They brought them home to the old man, his fair jewels; than whom earth's richest treasures in his sight had no price ; and told him he was childless and alone. It is a straice decree that the old plant should llius survive the stripling tilings it should and for whom it would have died a thousand tiroes. Is it surprising that 1 should wish to die in the mine V V oil have indeed,' I replied, 'drank of affliction. Whence did you derive consola- j tion ?' I lie old man looked up; from llcnven; ' God gave and he hath taken away, blessed Ire his name I bowed my head to the mi-
ner's pious prayer, and the old man passed on. Why are the ladies' gowns about the region of i he waist, like a camp meeting ? Because there is a great gulhciing there.

GRASP OF THE HUMAN MIND. Our earth, as is well known, has the form ofasphcriod, a little flattened towards the poles. Its radius is about 1500 leagues. The highest mountains do not rise to more than two leagues above the level of the sea, and there are hut a few tracts naturally situated below that rebel : and the greatest depths which have been reached by digging in the quarries, and more especially in the mines, do not exceed 1800 feet. The inequalities of the soil, then, are very trifling, when compared with the whole mass of the terrestial sphcriod ; and if the depths of the pits dug from the surface strike us with awe if the þÿ elevation of the mountains whose summits we perceive to be lost in the clouds, confound us

TasTJijra&isjR mainamasrea &xtiz+ with astonishment, it is only because we judge of them by comparison with the extreme smallness of the objects which surround us. þÿ The earth, the superficies of which seems so unequal and rugged, would offer to the eye of an individual, capable embracing of the outline at a glance, only the smooth appearance of one of our artificial globes, at the instant when it comes from the hands of the workman who has polished it. Let us suppose the terrestial spheriod to be represented by a ball three inches in diameter. If we wished upon this ball to figure, in relief, the inequalities which are seen upon the surface of the earth, the slightest protuberances, almost invisible to the eye, assisted by a microscope, would represent the highest mountains ; the slightest scratch which could be made on its surface would be deeper, in relation to its diameter, than are the greatest artificial cavities in proportion to that of the earth ; and the vapours which a single breath would cause to be condensed, would perhaps be too thick to represent the atmosphere, even to the height at which clouds are formed. þÿ For us, imperceptible atoms, who vegitate in this slight stratum of humid air, there is no expression to describe our littleness, and the weakness of our means, when we employ them to act upon the globe. Nevertheless, this puny atom, has measured the earth, the dimensions of which crush him to nothing ; he has measured the sun, a million times greater than the earth ; he has calculated the

distance which seperates it from that orb, whose brilliance his feeble gaze cannot sustain ; he has recognised in the myriads of " of the Leeward Islands to be elected on the stars which sparkle in the firmament, so many other suns spread through the immensity of the universe, among which revolve their re- " pected Packet, an bumble Memorial to our spective systems of opaque globes, all of whose movements they regulate. diminutiveness, of raising his ideas to an expanse without bounds, the earth is no more to his enlaiged conceptions than a grain of sand lost in the infinity of space. Is there not, in all this, matter for much reflection on the superiority of the human mind, which enables it to comprehend objects of such magnitude, though nature seems to have condemned it to vegitate within so narrow a circle 1 þÿ Bertrand's revolution of the Globe .

FEMALE LOVE. Emily was now in the happiest period of love þÿ perhaps its only happy one ; she felt a keener sense of enjoyment, a pleasure in trifles, a reliance on the present ; her step was more buoyant, her laugh more glad ; she felt a desire to be kind to all around, and her nature seemed all gaiety but for its sweetness. the proverb þÿ " Love's first steps are upon the rose," " its second finds the thorn says " þÿ Like the maiden of a fairy tale, we destroy our spell, when we open toexamine in what it þÿ characters it is written. In its ignorance is its happiness ; there is none of the anxiety that is the fever of hope þÿ no fears, for there is no calculation þÿ no selfishness, for it asks for nothing þÿ no disappointment, for nothing is expected ; it is like the deep quiet enjoyment of basking in the bright sunshine, without thinking of either how the glad warmth will ripen our fruits and flowers, or how the dark clouds in the distance forebode a storm. I doubt whether this morning twilight of the affections has the same intent of duration and influence in man that it has in woman; the necessity of exertion for attainment has

been early inculcated upon þÿhim he - knows that if lie could win he must Woo ; and his imagination acts ehieflv as a stimulus. But a woman's is of a more passive kind ; she has no motive for analysing feelings, whose future rests not with herself: more imaginative from early sedentary habits, she is content to dream on, and some chance reveals to herself the secret she would never have learnt from self investigation. Imbued with all the timidity, exalted by all the romance of a first attachment, never did a girl yet calculate on making what is called a conquest of the man she loves. A loves. A conquest is the resource of weariness þÿ the consolation of disappointment þÿ a second world of vanity and ambition, sighed for like Alexanders, but not till we have wasted and destroyed the heart's first sweet world of early love. Let Lord Bvron say what he will of bread and butter, girlhood is a beautiful season, and its love þÿ its warm, uncalculating, devoted love þÿ so exagerating in its þÿsimplicity so keen from its freshness þÿ is the very poetry of attachment; after years have nothing like it. To know that the love which once seemed eternal can have an end, destroys its immortality; and thus brought to a level with the beginnings and endings þÿ the chances and changes of life's common place employments and pleasures: and alas ! from the sublime to the ridiculous there is but a step þÿ ouf divinity turns out an idol þÿ we are grown too wise, too worldly for our former þÿfaith and we
laugh at what we wept at before ; such laughter is more þÿbitter a thousand times more bitter than tears."--- Romance and Rea \ 'y

In the dreams of delight, which with ardor we seek, Oft the phanton of sorrow appears; And the roses of pleasure, which bloom on the cheek, Must be steep'd in the dew of our tears. In the fountain of joy, when it sparkles most bright, Salt mixtures embitter the spring; Though its lustre may tremble through bow'rs of delight, In the draught disappointment will sting.
But if Heaven hath one source of enjoyment bestovv'd, Unmingled and sweet as its own, In the streams of affection its bounty hath flow'd, And there we may taste it alone.

But the pure, simple fount Love would seize as his prize, When commingled with passion's foul tide ; Though diminished in radiance, still lrotn our eyes, The poison of anguish may hide. Let friendship the stream, as it flows calm and clear, Receive unpolluted for me ; Or if tenderness mingled a sigh or a tear, The draught still the sweeter will be. Oh! g. ve mc the friend, in whose warm faithful breast The eigh breathes respensive to mine ; Where my cares can obtain the soft pillow of rest, And my sorrows may love to recline.
Not the friend who, suspicious of change or of guiie, Would shrink from a confidence free; Nor him who with fondness complacent can smile On the eye that looks calmly on me.
Not the friend who my hour of pleasure will share, But abides not the season of grief; Who flies from the brow that is darken'd by care, And the silence that looks for relief. S. i\ 0.

THE Bible Society. A letter having been received by the Reverend J. K. Bagger, from the Bishop of Zealand, acknowledging the sum last year remitted by Captain Keutsch, we deem it our duty to publish the following translation of it for the gratification of the Members o i the Society, and the promotion of the important object. C J. K. BAGGER. Secretaries < B. LUCKOCK. ( H. W. SYBRECHT. " For the valuable donation of $ 229 55ct, which your reverence, by your letter of 3d June transmitted from the Bible Society in St. Croix, through Captain Keetsch. to the Bible Society in Denmark, we tender you our grateful thanks, and consider this donation the more, as voluntary contributions to the Society have of late, been very rare. We greatly rejoice to learn by your letter, that the Bible Society is again established in the Island, and that several worthy Ladies have united to promote that Christian objeet; so that there is a well founded hope, that the Holy Scriptures will be more disseminated, and religion enlivened and nourished. We wish the Directors and Members of the Society the blessing of God upon their labours, and we will consider it as a sincere duty to contribute as far as is possible, to such humane and benevolent endeavours." (Signed) MYNSTER. Vice President.

St. Croix, CHRISTIAN STED, ( V/ ON DA Y) March 5, 1838. > »««- The second January mails from London reached this Island on Friday last ; London dates of the 1 5th January are received; the greatest, and Almost only article of interest in the papers is the total destruction by fire of the Royal Exchange of London on the night oj the 10th January. By this calamity, Lloyd's, and all the various establishments located in the greatest Commercial mart of the world, are levelled with the dust; the night was very cold, and the hoses oj the fire engines were frozen, so that considerable time elapsed before they could be used, the origin of the fire was supposed to be caused by the communication of healed air from the Jlues of the Stoves; |i< commenced in the rooms attached to Lloyd's , about 10 o'clock in the evening and burnt all night, the spacious area surrounded by wooden galleries affording fuel for the fames; the statues of nearly all the Kings of England, since William the Conqueror which were placed in Niches, are all destroyed ; the building contained u great amount of valuable documents, books, bonds and money deposited in the offices of Lloyd's underwriters and in those of stock brokers ( mostly in Iron safes,) which have been dug out of the ruins, and in many cases the papers and money recovered, uninjured; the Lord Mayor has offeied Guild Hall to the merchants, which has been accepted as a temporary Exchange, but it was supposed that the Draper's Hall would be leased 'till a new

Exchange could be built; the Bank of England would have been in great danger had the wind carried the fames in that direction The Royal Exchange was built of Brick by Sir reign oj Queen Elisabeth It was burnt exact- Thomas Gresham in the year 1500, in the . ly a century afterwards in the great fire of London of 1660; it was rebuilt of Portland Stone in the reign of Charles 2d, it formed an oblong Quadrangle 205 feet by 110; it is stated that £ 1 50,000 Stlg. will be required to rebuild it. Canada was still the great subject of interest ia England; very considerable reinforcement of troops were to he sent there , and an augmentation of 20,000 men to the regular army was in contemplation. The decease of the venerable Lord Eldon in his 87th year is announced ; he was, with the exception of Lord Lyndoch, the oldest peer in England, and for many years Lord Chancellor of Great Britain.

The Charte de 1830 of last night contained the following telegraphic despatch : " Bayonne, Jan. 3. " On the 29th, Basilio Garcia traversed the Ebro at Alcanadra. near Logrono, with eight battalions arid 200 cavalry; 1000 men of ed, or drowned themselves " tiiis force refused to pass the ford and desert- This despatch, then, contradicts the news reported a few days since of the Carlist ex pedition having been defeated. Don Basilio Garcia, far from having been defeated by the Christines, effected the passage of the Ebro at the ford of Alcanadra, near Mendavia, in the night ot the 28th of December. He had with liirn about 6000 men As to the desertion and drowning mentioned in the above despatch, we must wait a few days for further intelligence before we place much confidence in this report. Letters from Bavonne of January 5, state tiiat the reported affair of Mendavia has not been confirmed. The only thing believed there to be certain was, that Garcia had lost many men in crossing the Ebro. and that when on the opposite side lie found other obstacles winch prevented him from taking the road to Soria. Another letter from Bayonne states, that Don Carlos had not left Llodio on the 31st of Dec The valley ot La Mena was occupied bv Carlist divisions, 3000 Carlist infantry, and 2000 cavalry passed the Ebro, in the neighbourhood ol Lodesa, without being op-

posed by Kibera, whose troops were within ten leagues of them. The Phare de Bayonne announces that the baitalion ot the English marines at Passages is about to embark, to proceed to Halifax, wore they are to be employed against the insurgents of Canada Letters from Madrid of the 31st ult state that General Oraa has resigned his functions ot Commander in Chief of the army of the Centre ; and he bases his resignation on the refusal of the Government to giant him the number of troops without which he must remain but a passive spectator of the excesses committed by the bands of Cabrera and others. He is now retained at Valencia and Morviedo. Who will supercede him is not known. PARIS, Jan 9. sian army in the Caucasus, commanded by the

Baron de Rosen in person, has met with a severe check between Derbent and Rouinuki. Each author has his allotted nightly share of the receipts, whenever any one of the pieces composed by him is acted, and his claims descend to his familv or heirs. A piece, therefore, that keeps the stage, becomes a lamily estate, and those, the merits of which are slight or transient, have their proportionate reward. Beaumarchais, after having received seven hundred thousand livros, (about twenty nine thousand pounds sterling,) for La Folic Journee, gave it iu perpetuity.

The Memory of Guttenberg. þÿ The printer Guttenberg. who it is claimed by some to bo the first who executed the art, was borne at Mayence, on the Rhine. According to the late German papers, a festival in honor of his memory was to be celebrated at that place on the 24th of June. It was expected to be attended by numbers from all parts of the world. Some of the more morbid of the German journals grumble at this, maintaining that it is doubtful, from the number of bad books, and worse newspapers, which the art has called into existence, whether another fate than that of deification ought not to be awarded to its discoverer.

From Galignan's Messenger. Our readers may recollect that, in February last, we gave an account of a woman, named B , burning a considerable amount in bank notes, and other property, in order to prevent her husband retiring into the country, as he proposed to do. This monomania of destruction has seized her again and has ended only with her life. During the i Frederikstod's Police Office, Feb: 20, 1838. night of the 30th ult., she commenced by burning in the chimney all her linen, clothes, and every article in her chamber. She then broke six panes of glass, threw all the earthenware and china out of the window, and after sewing up the bottom part of her dress, threw herself from the window of the second floor into the street, by which she broke a leg and an arm. On being taken up. and placed in her bed, she expressed no regret for what she had done, refused the attendance of the ministers of religion, tore off with her teeth the bandages which were placed bv the surgeon, and died in seven hours afterwards.

THE Bible Society. A letter having been received by the Reverend J. K. Bagger, from the Bishop of .Zealand, acknowledging the sum last year remitted by Captain Keutsch, we deem it our duty to publish the following translation of it for the gratification of the Members of the Society, and the promotion of the important object. ( J. K BAGGER. Secretaries < B. LUCKOCK. ( H. W. SY ERE CUT. " For the valuable donation of $ 229 55ct, which your reverence, by your letter of 3d June transmitted from the Bible Society in St. Croix, through Captain Keutsch, to the Bible Society in Denmark, we tender you our grateful thanks, and consider this donation the more, as voluntary contributions to the Society have of late, been very rare. We greatly rejoice to learn by your letter, that the Bible Society is again established in the Island, and that several worthy Ladies have united to promote that Christian object ; so that there is a well founded hope, that the Holy Scriptures will be more disseminated, and religion enlivened and nourished. We wish the Directors and Members of the Society the blessing of God upon their labours, and we will consider if as a sincere duty to contribute as lar as is possible, to such humane and benevolent endeavours." (Signed) MYNSTER. Vice President.

Bank of St. Thomas. (communicated.) The dividend of 8f per cent, now payable on the paid up Capital of Ihe Bank of Saint Thomas, is much short of what it was expected to be. þÿ About two months ago, and since then, it was very generally said, that the clear gain of the Bank for the first year, was eighteen per cent on the paid up Capital, after deducting all charges, and something as a reserve, to meet any unforeseen losses, that might arise out of transactions not closed. The paid up Capital of the Bank appears to be about 150,000 þÿ the current reports, since it began business, have been, that the sum deposited with it, at interest, for short and long periods, was much greater than its paid up Capital, and that it had latterly refused deposits, at interests, in consequence of its being unable to employ to advantage, the amount of funds it already possessed. Taking the deposits at 8210,000 and the circulation at 840,009, the working funds of the Bank have amounted to about 8400,000 in 1837 þÿ keeping this in view, the apparent gain of about 815,000 on such a capital or fund, during 12 months, certainly is very trifling, and as about one half of it is said to have arisen from an exchange of money, and from damages on returned bills, both of them mere temporary sources of profit, not likely to continue in time coming, the future prospects of the Shareholders are not very encouraging ; the small sum of 2000 dollars set aside as a reserve to meet any loss, is scarcely worthy of notice.

The Bank of Jamaica paid a dividend, at the rate of about 14 per cent a year, nearly 0 mouths ago. The Bank of British Guiana is now paying a dividend of, it is believed, about ten per cent being the first one. The Colonial Bank will not probably pay more than a nominal dividend þÿ < to fus1. ss here has been limited, and cannot have been profitable, while among the small British Colonies there will not likely be any profit; the want of profit may be accounted for, by the expensive scale on which the Colonial Bank has been established in the Colonies, and by other circumstances. The Parent Bank may therefore soon find it necessary, to discontinue one or more of the most unproductive branches in the West Indies, and to adopt improvements in the mode of conducting some of the others, with a view to make them productive to the Bank, and beneficial to the places in which they are established. The following notices appear in a Liverpool paper of the 1 1th January from the 4 Banks mentioned, all of which have been established within the last few years ; Liverpool Banking Company þÿ a dividend of six per cent for the half year ending 30th December 1837, payable at the Bank on the J 8th January 1838. Liverpool Union Bank þÿ a dividend of four per cent, for the half year ending 31st Dec. 1837, on the Capital Stock, payable on and after the 1st of March 1838. Liverpool Borough Bank þÿ a dividend of live per cent, for the half year, on the paid Up Capita! of the Company, payaole on and
after the 31st January 1838, being the third dividend. Bank of Liverpool þÿ a dividend for the half year from the 1st July to the 3 1st Dec. 1837, the rate of ten per cent per annum, on the

increased paid up Capital of the Company, payable at the Bank on and after the 1st of February 1838, being the eleventh dividend. None of the Banks mentioned above issue notes þÿ they trade upon their own paid up Capital, and receive money on deposit, for which they pay interest ; it is payable at all times on demand. At the Sixtli annual general meeting of the proprietors of the Bank of Liverpool, held on the 13th September 1837, the following statement was presented by the Directors : The paid up Capital of the Company, on the 30th June 1837, was £381,400 The premium on 1734 shares, sold & carried to the reserved surplus fund, amounted to 26,010 The nett profits of the year, after tin current r-xpences, and provision tor bad and doubtful debts, amounted to 35,090 The Proprietors have received two half yearly dividends of 0 per cent, each 45,G97 towards which £10,607 was withdrawn from the reserved surplus fund. The reserved surplus fund upwards of 106,000 At the same period of 1836, it was 190,722 The Directors recommend, that they be authorized to carry the sum of £95.365 from the reserved fund to the Capital account, thereby adding £2 10 0, or 25 per cent to the Stock of each Shareholder, being satisfied, that in a reserved tund of 100,000, there is ample provision for all probable contingencies. St. Thomas, 7th Match 1838.

From the Barbadian, February 25 1838. By the arrival on Wednesday last of her Majesty's packet Sheldrake , Lieutenant Passingham, 35 days from Falmouth, with the second January mails, we are put in possession of London and other English dates to the loth ultimo. It is with great regret we communicate to our readers accounts of the melancholy destruction of that noble pile of building, the Boyal Exchange of London, which was burnt down on the night of Wednesday the 10th of last month Full particulars ol this occurrence are given in our columns ol to-day ; and the short extract hereunto appended will give our readers some idea of the extent of the calamity, which may almost be considered a national one. As yet it would seem nothing is known of the origin of the fire : "lor many years London has not been visited by so calamitous a fire as that which broke out on Wednesday night at the Royal Exchange. Of the whole of that noble building there remains nothing but the charred and ruined skeleton ! The structure itself is totally destroyed, and the value rather than the actual amount of property consumed is beyond calculation. As vet nothing certain is know n of the origin of this disastrous occurrence. Five hours from the outbreak of the conflagration there remained but a smoking mass of ruins in the place of that Exchange which, since the reign of Charles If., has been one of the most beautiful specimens of our metropolitan architecture. It would be quite impossible to form any idea of the quantity of property destroyed; but from its
nature and extent, we fear the greatest and most complicated embarrassments must be

produced. The firtst battalion of the Grenadier Guards, whose good conduct during the night deserves great praise, remained on the spot until nipe o'clock next morning when they were relieved by a number of Special constables, &c. During the fire the bridges over the T hames were crowded with people, and the flames were distinctly visible at Windsor Castle, a distance of 24 miles from Cornhill. An Essex farmer states that the lire was seen at Thoydonmount, near Epping, 18 miles from London. On the high lands of Surrey, within 10 miles of the metropolis, the progress of the conflagration was observed by the astonished country people, who watched the destruction of the tower when the flames ascended that part of the edifice. It was a grand and awful sight, and will not soon be forgotten by those who viewed it. þÿ One of the most remarkable circumstances connected with the fire is the fact that at twelve o'clock, when the flames had just reached the north-west angle of the building, and were rapidly making their way to the tower, the chimes struck up, as usual at that hour, the old tune, " There's nue luck about the house," and continued for five minutes. '1 be effect was extiaordinary, and the tune was distinctly heard : alas, it was the lost time ! The silver-toned bells, whose joyful notes in playing at intervals of every three hours, " God save the Queen," " Life let us cherish," " There's nae luck about the house," and on Sundays the old 101th Psalm, have so often gladdened the hearts of the citizens,

and amused the frequenters of Change, are silent for þÿever melted by the intense heat or broken to pieces The clock had a very singular effect while the tower was burning. The plates of the dials were red-hot, and the hands pointed to the hour, 25 minutes past one, when the works took fire, melting the chime barrels and the machinery in a few minutes, The Lord Mayor has ordered the Guildhall to be thrown open for the accommodation of merchants who attend the Exchange." Major General Sir Amos N'orcott died at Cork on Monday the 8th ultimo. This distinguished officer had recently been relieved from the command of the Southern District, Ireland, in consequence of indisposition. The official correspondence of the government, relating to the disturbances in Canada, has been published, comprising a series of despatches from Lord Glenclg to the Earl of Gosford.

The day previous to his sailing, Sir George was presented with a splendid service of plate of the value of £1,500, bv the colony of Van Dienrian s land þÿ the principal articles bearing the following inscription : þÿ " To Colonel fiff George Arthur, li. Ere the eye of a single reader has rested on these lines, the mortal remains of our Governor and Ruler, Sir James Carmichaei, Smyth, Bart, will have been gathered, amid the regret of sorrowing hundreds to their kindred dust. Sir James departed this life at Camp House yesterday afternoon, at 10 minutes past 6 o'clock, after a briet illness of but three days. In recording this melancholy event, that Journal which has so often, from conscientious motives, opposed the late Governor in his policy, not only now and for ever forgets all formei points of difference, but also steps forward to bear a willing testimony to the many good qualities of the deceased. Let his epitaph, as we would inscribe it, bear þÿ alone of his virtues and his good acts record be his failings (and who are free from fault ?) forgotten as the earth closes over his mortal career. It cannot be denied that to our late Governor this Colony is indebted for very many highly beneficial measures. In the first place, whatever may have been, and indeed still are, the ditferences of opinion respecting his Excellency's policy on the eventful change whieh took place in this Colony in August 1834, it is at least certain that he succeeded | aught hut the deepest sympathy to an eminent degree in successfully carrying through this measure, with as little of popular commotion and human suffering as the most sanguine could have anticipated. That a course of greater energy at that frying and critical lime would have been more politic, is

still our opinion, and, we think, would have been attended with even more satisfactory results than ensued from the measures his late Excellency then deemed it adviseable to þÿpursue; the result, however, if not as satisfactory as it was possible to have renderec it, was at least sufficiently so to claim for his Excellency from this Colony, as it has already elicited from the Imperial Government, a warm and lasting gratitude, shedding a halo over his memory, and gilding his name on his cenotaph as a benefactor of his kind. Another favourable point in his late Excellency's public career in administering the Government of this Colony, should not be forgotten at this moment. He infused into the Councils of his administration a degree of energy and a spirit of reform, which could alone have arisen from a strong mind and an able head like his own. He struck at corruption wherever he met with it with uncompromising determination þÿ he reformed our Civil list in a spirit of rigid, but fair economy þÿ and he abolished various sinecure offices which had hitherto existed but as sources of corrupt patronage. These acts of benefit did his late Excellency perform to this Colony, þÿ and though we duly recorded them when they occurred, yet it is now, at this sad moment, a source of melancholy gratification to us again to dwell upon these good deeds of departed greatness. And truly with what a feeling of satisfaction may we not remember that the closing act of his public career was

and that when last in the Council Chamber of his Government, he ordered relief to he granted to the widowed and the desolate þÿ he gave shelter to the orphans, and poured the halm of charity upon the bruised spirit of the mourner. We need not further particularize the instance we above allude to, than refer to 'lie report of the Colonial Legislative pro-

..ah- irtl ceedings, where will be seen recorded the case of a poor widow, in arrears for taxes, to whom his late Excellency ordered relief out of the Extraordiuaries It was a hail of benevolence in his late Excellency's character never to be forgotten Tarty prejudice, or political bias might have led him into errors ol judgment and of action, and for these the bent of þÿeducation the consequences of peculiar associations, or the chapter ot accidents alone are liable, but here was an act ol spiritaneous benevolence entirely arising from a good heart and a charitable spirit. W be have hitherto confined our imperfect remarks on the public career of his late Excellency to that period of his life in which lie governed þÿhere and we need scarce extend them further, as the annals of his country speak the rest: þÿ they tell of a brave and sagacious Soldier, who closed his active life of military renown and honor on the same field that gave to Europe freedom, and to despotism a grave þÿ the Plains of Waterloo: þÿ in which eu agement we believe his late Excellency was in command of the Engineers, a corps iu winch, if we are rightly informed, he originally entered the service. We touch not the relations of private life save but to commend. 'The sorrows there felt for such a loss are too sacred to cause and the sincerest commiseration. The veil that shrouds the now desolate hearth of the departed one is raised but for one moment to tell the reader how blameless he was in private life, and

therefore hovv fit an example for hi n to imitate. Teace be to his þÿmanes may his virtues and his greatness be recorded by abler pens than ours þÿ no commeiiuaiioii, however, is so sincere as that which is willingly rendered to departed worth by one who never flattered it when living. His Excellency's remains were this afternoon accompanied to their tomb by almost every respectable inhabitant ol the town and its neighbourhood, lie was, of course, buried wiili military honors, as became a man who had lived and died a soldier, and the thunders of those guns the departed knew so well how to direct against the enemies of his country, peeled an appropriate requiem over his grave. From the New York Commercial Advertiser , March 8, 1838. MEETING AT THE EXCHANGE. The meeting of the merchants at the Exchange this afternoon, was numerously attended. It was called to order by Ciiari.es H. Russule, Esq , on whose motion J A M ES BOOR- MAN, Esq., was appointed Chairman, and JAMES LEE and JONATHAN STUR- GES., chosen Secretaries. The following resolutions, offered by Pelatiafi Perit, Esq., and seconded by Samuel W aro, Esq., were thereupon read and unanimously adopted : þÿ Resolved, That this meeting hails with great satisfaction the declaration on the part of the New York city banks of their purpose to resume specie payments on or before the 10th of May next. Resolved, That we have entire confidence in the solidity of our banks, and in their ability to resume and maintain specie payments, and that in this measure we will give them our cordial arid active co-operation Resolved, That independently of moral obligation and legislative enactment, the favorable state of foreign exchanges and the diminished liabilities both of banks and individuals, call for a prompt resumption of specie payments, and we consider such a course the surest means of equalizing ultimately our internal exchanges and of restoring general prosperity. Resolved, That in contemplating the resumption of specie payments, we can perceive no reason to apprehend that it will occasion any further contraction on the part of the Banks ; but, on the contrary, that the restoration of confidence, which must necessarily grow out of that measure, will lead to

a gradual increase of their issues, and enable them to extend greater facilities to the community. Resolved, That regarding the general resumption of specie payments by the banks throughout the United States as essential to our national credit abroad, and as calculated to regulate our internal exchanges, we respectfully invite the institutions of other states to a simultaneous effort to accomplish this most desirable object.

PLAN FUR PACIFYING CANADA. Extract oj a letter from Lord Glenelg to the Earl of Durham, (I. C. B. dated Downingstreet, Jan. 20, 1838. In order to lay the ground for the permanent settlement of the questions which agitate Lower Canada, and also of those which create divisions between Upper and Lower Canada, it will probably be found necessary to resort to some legislative measures of a comprehensive nature. But before such mca. sures can be framed and submitted to Parliament, it would be highly desirable to ascertain the wishes and opinions of the people of both provinces regarding them. This object could best be attained by a personal communication on your part with such persons selected from each province as may be presumed, from their station, character, and influence, to represent the feelings of their fellow-countrymen in general. It seems advisable, therefore, to authorize your lordship, if you should so think fit, to call around you a certain number of such persons, with whom you might take counsel on the most important affairs of the two provinces; the

®A5J3!E. TaSTJHTIMSIR 303aMITB3 AT33» time of meeting of such committee of advice being left entirely to your discretion. You are, therefore, empowered to select three members from the Legislative Council of Upper Canada to attend such meeting ; and to invite the House of Assembly of Upper Canada to nominate ten of the members for the same purpose Under ordinary circumstances, the same course would be pursued with respect to the Legislature of Lower Canada. But if the bill now before Parliament should be passed into a law, recourse must be had, during the suspension of that Legislature, to another mode of supplying the deficiency. You will, accordingly, during such suspension, select three members of the body at present composing the Legislative Council, and will take measures for calling on the electors in each of the five districts into which Lower Canada is now divided, to elect two persons to sit in the Committee. Your Lordship can obviate any difficulty which may stand in the way of holding such elections, by an ordinance for this purpose, to be passed by the authority of the Governor in Council. The Committee will thus consist of twentysix members, over whose deliberations you will of course preside. The Committee being thus formed, you will bring before them the subjects on which you desire to receive their opinion and advice Among the most important of these are the question in debate between the two Canadian Provinces. In the last session, both Houses of Parliament passed a resolution, " That great incon-

venience has been sustained by his Majesty's subjects inhabiling the Provinces of Lower and Upper Canada, from the want of some adequate means for regulating and adjusting questions respecting the trade and commerce of the said provinces, and divers other questions wherein the said provinces have a common interest, and it is expedient that the Legislatures of the said provinces respectively be authorized to make provision for the joint regulation and adjustment of such their common interests." It is clear that some plan must be devised to meet the just demands of Upper Canada. It will be for your Lordship, in conjunction with the Committee, to consider if this should not be done by constituting some joint legislative authority, which should preside over all questions of common interest to the two provinces, and which might be appealed to in extraordinary cases, to arbitrate between contending parties in either; preservingt however, to each province its distinct Legislature, with authority in all matters of exclusively domestic concern. If this should be your opinion, you will have farther to consider what should be the nature and limits of such authority, and all the particulars which ought to be comprehended in any scheme for its establishment. The constitutional act of 1791 will supply another subject of deliberation, with the view to determine what measures may safely be taken to correct the defects which have hitherto interfered, at least in the lower province,

with its successful working. The constitution of the Legislative Council has formed the chief topic of complaint with the House of Assembly of Lower Canada, and they have insisted that the only remedy is to tie found in making the council elective. On this subject the following resolution was last tear passed by both Houses of Parliament: " That in the existing state of Lower Canada, it it

unadvisable to make the Legislative Council of that province an elective body, but it is expedient that measures be adopted for securing to that branch of the Legislature a greater degree of public confidence." It will be for you and the committee to consider in what manner the judgment thus pronounced by Parliament can best be carried into effect. There are other very importaat subjects regarding which you will probably þÿ it right to consult the same advisers, such, think for example, as the provision that should be made to meet the necessary expenses of the civil government in Lower Canada þÿ the state of the law affecting the tenure of landed property in that province þÿ the establishment of a court for the trial of appeals and impeachments. There is, in truth, not one of the many interesting questions relating to the good government and well-being of the two Canadas, which might not very properly engage the attention of the committee. On all the subjects which I have specified, and on others which may come under the notice of the Committee, your Lordship will probably have to recommend the adoption of some legislative measures in this country. You will transmit to me an explanation of such measures in the fullest detail, in order that the Government may consider of the propriety of submitting them to Parliament. You are authorised to fix the times and places of the meetings of the Committee, to adjourn them from time to time, and to frame all regulations necessary for the dispatch of
business, You arc also empowered to dissolve the Committee at your pleasure.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, March 13, 1838. LATER FROM FRANCE.

By the Havre packet Louis Philippe Gastoff, sailed February 1st, we have Paris files to the 31st of January and Havre to the 1st of February, both inclusive. The Paris papers mention several arrests of private " hell-keepers," who have opened establishments since the closing of the great public houses. At one of these houses 18,000 francs were found in the bank, and seized, with the tables, furniture, clocks, &c. By the law suppressing gaming houses, all these are forfeited to the state. It waS reported in Paris on the 31st of January, that .another conflagration had broken out at St. Petersburgh þÿ in the pa lace of the Grand Duke Michael. A letter from Frankfort, of the 28th, announces the destruction, by fire, of the palace occupied by the Duke Alexaneer of Wirtemburgh, recently married to the Frincess Marie of France. Nothing was saved but the jewels of the Duchess, and a few of the most valuable articles of furniture. The fire broke out at midnight, and the Duke and Duchess were compelled to fly» wrapped in cloaks, not having time to dress.

From the New Orleans Bee, March 5. IMPORTANT FROM MEXICO. The schooner Levin Jones, arrived at this port, sailed from Vera Cruz on the 20th ult. þÿ Two French brigs of war had arrived, and the remainder of a squadron, 14 in all, were expected, to enforce the French claims, a part of which had been admitted. Fortifications had been commenced to protect the town in case of bombardment, which was expected. The French brigs of war were moored in the Island of Sacrificiss, in one of thein was the Baron Defliindos, minister from France, who bad left Mexico early in January. A squadron of ten frigates and ships was daily expected, but it waa believed that every thing would be settled amicably, particularly if the system proposed by Gomez Farias was pursued. In the mean time the French are watched continually by the populace, and their position is rendered highly perilous by the continual insults and menaces to which they are subjected. The arrival of the squadron is greatly needed in order to obviate the contemplated excess.

The Earl of Durham it is said will not go out to his important government until April. Mr. Ellicc, it is supposed, will accompany his Lordship as his Private Secretary. þÿ John Col bourne has been made a Knight Grand Cross of the Bath. The winter in England, by the latest dates, was intensely cald. The river Thames was so frozen that almost all navigation was impeded. Although an ox had not yet been roasted on the river, as was the case in the winter of 1813-14, yet, a sheep was roasted whole in the centre of the river the latter end of January. Various articles were exhibited for sale, as at a Fair ; and four gentlemen Irom Mincing Lane had a table placed about 100 yards from the shore, and amused themselves with playing several rubbers of whist. There had been several instances of loss of life among persons who ventured on places where the ice was not thick. þÿ Barbadian, March 17.

From the Barbados Mercury, March 17, 1838 THE COLONIAL BANK. Beport by the Directors of the Colonial Bank incorporated by Hoyui Charter) to the Proprietors, assembled at the first general meeting held at the City of London Tavern, on the 25th January, 1838. It being provided bv the charter of the colonial bank, that a general meeting of the proprietors shall be held at this time for the election of five directors and one auditor, the directors have, in the discharge of their duty, called the proprietors together for that purpose, and they avail themselves of the opportunity to lay before them a report of their proceedings. From the recent commencement of business in the West Indies they can do little more than detail measures which have been taken to attain the important objects proposed in the formation of this corporation. It is deemed unnecssary to enter into a detail of the negociations which were carried on with his late majesty's government in procuring the charter, being it sufficient to state that they were brought to a successful conclusion, on the 1st June, 1830, on which day the charter received the great seal. On the same day Mr. James M'Queen, the gentleman who, from his known experience and popularity in the West Indies, had been selected by the directors to visit the colonies, and to make preliminary arrangements for the establishment of branches, left London on the prosecution of his mission. He proceeded in tiie first instance to Jamaica, and after having concluded part of the necessary arrangements in that Island, he

went to Barbados. Mr. M'Queen, accompanied by Mr. Michael M'Chlery (who having been manv years established at Barbados in connection with ! one of the first mercantile houses in that Island, has been selected to fill the office of manager of that important station,) then proceeded on a joint mission to British Guiana, Trinidad, and most of the other British Colonics, as also the Island of St. Thomas, and made arrangements for commencing business whenever it might seem expedient to the directors to give instructions for so doing. Alter this Mr. M'Queen again visited Jamaica to complete the arrangements there, and finally returned to London on the 8th May, 1837. As soon as the directors were in possession of intelligence that the branches at Jamaica (Kingston), Barbados, British Guiana, Trinidad, and St Thomas were in a sufficient state of forwardness to lead them to expect I that business could be commenced upon the Sir | necessary funds being lodged at those places, they made the call of 1 51. per share, in compliance with that clause in the charter, which required, that one fourth of the capital, or 500,0001., should be actually paid up previous to the commencement of business. On the 18th May the directors had the satisfaction of announcing to the Secretary of State for the Colonies, and to the Chancellor of tiie Exchequer, that on the 13th the sum of 500.0001 had been paid up. Agreeably to instructions previously sent to them, the above-mentioned branches open-

ed for business on the 15th þÿMay the branch at St Vincent on the 3d July, and those at Grenada, Antigua, Tobago, St. Kitts, Dominica, and St. Lucia on the first of August. Agencies have subsequently been established at Forto Rico and St. Croix.

Since the opening of the head bank at Kingston, Jamaica, a branch has been established at Montego Bay, and agencies at Falmouth, Savaa-na-la-Mar, and Morant Bay, in that Island. The directors have much satisfaction in stating that they have been extremely fortunate in their selection of managers and officers ; and that all these establishments are under the management of gentlemen of great local knowledge and commercial experience, assisted by officers and cierks of the greatest respectability. Agents have been appointed at New York, and in the British North American Colonies. The directors cannot conclude their report without adverting to the difficulties they have had to contend with in the commencement of their operations, arising from the very defective arid unsound state of the currency in the West Indies generally, and the imperfect state of the law relating to legal tender for debt. Tbev have long been in communication with the government on this important subject, and they have now reason to hope that, ere long, the currency in the West Indies will be settled upon an uniform and sound basis, which will prove no less beneficial to the Colonial public than to the bank. They deem it proper also to allude to the establishment of rival banks in Jamaica, Demerara, and St. Thomas, and doing so, to declare their conviction that this institution will find no difficulty in securing a full share of the business liansacted in those colonics. The directors have likewise had to contend

with the prejudices invariably felt by all comj munities against institutions, the objects and operations of which are new and not well understood They fully anticipate, however, that these prejudices will soon give way before the real advantage in point of security, convenience, and punctuality which are offered by the bank. The first balance of the books of the corporation in the West Indies will have taken place on the 31st December last, and as it cannot be received from thence until the middle or end of next month, it is not in the power of the directors to lay before tiie present meeting any statement of the result of the operations of the bank. But it may be satisfactory to the proprietors to know, that the directors, judging from the returns of business that they are in possession of, entertain every expectation of having it in their power to produce at the next general meeting, in July, such a statement of profits as will enable them to declare a satisfactory dividend. The directors look forward to this result with the more confidence from the crisis in the United Stales which necessarily affected the pecuniary transactions of the West India Colonies, having passed away þÿ from the gradual restoration of confidence in that country þÿ and from the return of commercial affairs generally to a more sound and healthy condition On the motion of D. Solomons, Esq., seconded by Sir George Carroll, it was resolved unanimously, " That the report of the directors, which had been read, should be received."

On the motion of S, Gurney, Esq , seconded by E. l.ousada, Esq., it was resolved unanimously, " That the thanks of this meeting be given to the court of directors for then iiinemitting zeal and attention to the interests of the corporation."

London dates of the 15th February pr. packet, are received since our last. þÿ The Canada bill had received the Royal assent, somewhat modified, by the House of Lords. þÿ Mr. Roebuck had been heard at the bar of that house, and in a speech of two hours he defended the revolted Canadians, and severely censured the ministers. þÿ The House of Commons was engaged in appointing Committees on the contested elections. þÿ The poor lawbill for Ireland, strongly opposed by Mr. O'Connell, passed the Commons by a large majority, only 25 voting with O'Connell þÿ A motion to extend the right of suffrage was supported by the whole radical party and opposed by the ministers, and lost, yeas 107 þÿ nays 220 þÿ in this instance the ministers owred their majority to the conservatives, of whom 120 voted with them. In Spain Espartero attacked the Carlists in very strong positions near Balmaceda on the 30th January, and altho' repulsed three times, he finally succeeded in turning their left, and forcing them to retreat, thus re- þÿ lieving that place, which the Carlists had besieged. The cold weather in London had began to moderate, and the ice in the Thames to break up, þÿ thus permitting a great many icebound ships to enter and leave the docks ; þÿ but the weather has been stormy, in the Northern seas ; and many disasters had be- þÿ fallen navigation. The London Times of 15th February announces the shipwreck of the French Frigate Terpsichore. Capt- Le Tourneur from Martinique bound to France ; þÿ she was w recked

near Cork, coast of Ireland, having previously thrown her guns and many valuable articles overboard. Admiral De Mackau late Gov. Gen. of the French Islands was on board. A British Government Steamer was immediately dispatched to the aid and assistance of the crew, on learning of the disaster. The Bullion in the bank of England had increased to nine millions and a half sterling, and money was so plenty in London as to be easily obtained at 2 pr cent pr Annum on good securities. A committee of the merchants had waited on the Chancellor of the Exchequer to request Government assistance in rebuilding the Royal Exchange, which would no doubt be granted. The average price of British Island Muscovado Sugar in London Feb. 10th was 39s. and 6d. Stlg. in bond þÿ duty unpaid. þÿ ooo«- From the Barbados Mercury , March 20, 1838.

MACKENZIE, THE REBEL IN UPPER CANADA. ( From the Greenock Advertiser .) Mackenzie, the insurgent leader in Upper Canada, is, we should suppose, about 55 years of age. He is a native of Aberdeen, and has resided in the Canadas about It! or 18 years. For some time he paid very fervent court to Lord Dalhousie ; but that nobleman not meeting his advances with the return he expected, he became one of his lordship's bitter denouncers. He established a newspaper called the Colonial Advocate , in Toronto (then called York), the capital of Upper Canada It was distinguished alike for the violence of its political sentiments and its gross personalities þÿ His character for veracity among his contemporaries of the same line of politics, may be inferred from the fact that the Editor of the Canadian Freeman, a radical paper, was wont to change bis name from William Lion Mackenzie into William Lie-on Mackenzie. About twelve years ago, during the administration of Sir Peregrine Maitland, to which he was violently opposed, Mackenzie attacked not the public acts merely, but the private conduct and domestic arrangements of his political opponents þÿ a course of conduct which so exasperated the younger members of their families, that certain of them assembled in a riotous manner, and having broken into his printing office, they destroyed his press and threw his types into Lake Ontario. At the time when this highly improper proceeding took place, Mackenzie had crossed over to the United States, for the purpose of removing thither permanently, his journal in

Toronto being far from a profitable speculation. No sooner, however, did he hear of the riotous destruction of his property than he saw the advantages to be derived from it, and he instantly returned and raised an action of damages against those who were concerned in it. The jury, with the view no doubt of marking their sense of the impropriety of the conduct of the defendants, gave damages to fully ten times the amount of the injury sustained, which placed Mackenzie in far better circumstances than ho ever was iri before. He resumed his newspaper after a short time, and to some extent admitted his siris of personalities, and promised amendment. He has ever since conducted the paper, and has all along professed himself an

admirer of the United States form of go. vernment. He also got himself elected as one of the representatives for the country of York and mayor of Toronto. At the last election, however, he was rejected from both places, and has since been traversing the pro. vince, trying to get up grievance petitions lor his friend and correspondent Mr. Joseph Hume. The circumstance that the governor has offered £1000 currency for his apprehension reminds us of a passage in his history, which occurred about eight years ago. Early in the season he proceeded to Montreal, On his way to Quebec, and embarked in the steamer Waterloo, which was the first vessel that tried to make the passage that year. It had been reported that the ice bad broken up, and that the passage was open, but after proceeding a certain length the steamer got jammed among some pieces of ice which stove her sides in þÿ and but for the support afforded by their pressure, she would have gone to the bottom with, most probably, all on board. þÿ As it happened no lives were lost, the crew and passengers getting on shore upon the floating ice. Mackenzie wrote and transmitted to his newspaper a full and very interesting account of this accident. One of his brother journalists, of the same line of politics, made the narrative the subject of an editorial article, in which he detailed the various remarks which he alleged were made upon the catastrophe, and Mackenzie's safety. Many were said to have expressed astonishment at the escape of such a Jonah, on whose iniqui-

ties they laid the blame of the disaster ; but, he added, that he felt no such astonishment at Mackenzie's escape, as he had faith in an old proverb, which affirmed that ' he who was born to be hanged would never be drow n ed." The above anecdote will at once give the reader a specimen of the editorial courtesies current among Upper Canada journalists, and some idea of the respect in which Mr. Mackenzie was held by those who knew him pretty 'veil. He is a person of restless activity, and possessed of an inordinate portion of assurance. His vanity must have been very much mortified by his failure at the last election, but we never could have supposed that he would have taken any step so directly calculated to realize the sinister prediction of his brother editor as to head a rebellion. þÿ The sum offered as a reward for his apprehension if bestowed upon himself, would make him a very loyal and obedient subject. He will not find his present speculation such a profitable affiiir as the destruction of his printing establishment. þÿ Ibid.

A party of 250 ladies belonging to the Parish of St. Antoine, celebrated on the 30th Nov., the love of country and their patriotism, by a public dinner, from which every imported article was rigidly excluded. Various patriotic toasts and sentiments, appropriate to the spirit of the time, were proposed. A guard of honour, composed of 40 men belonging to the parish was in attendance with their muskets, and occasionally complimented the fair party by firing a J'eu de joie. So far from being frightened by the smell of powder or the roar of musketry, many of the ladies to prove that they can act in case of need, took muskets and discharged them with the most admirable tact and courage. þÿ Montreal Vindicator. It set forth that several years ago the precise time unknown a great number of cotton-spinners formed themselves into a combination for the purpose of keeping up the price of wages ; and, more effectually to attain their object, they administered to each other a secret oath binding the members to execute every task which the majority might impose ; and the said association resolved from time to time to strike work, and on these occasions they appointed certain of their number to be a guard committee to wratch the cotton mills where work was struck, and by means of menaces, molestation, and threats, to deter others from working in said mills þÿ of which several specific instances were brought forward ; and, that the perpetrators of said crimes might escape justice, they procured law-agents, or other persons, to become cautioners in the bailbond required to be executed for the appearance of the accused to stand trial, and placed in their hands the amount in money of the penalty to be paid in forfeiture by the flight and fugitation of the accused. Weight of Silk Worms. þÿ When newly hatched, it takes 54.536 silk worms to weigh an ounce. Alter the casting of the skin 3340 worms will make up the ounce After the second change 610 weigh an ounce. In the week passing between the second and third ages, the number of insects required to make up the same weight is 145. During the fourth age 35 worms weigh an ounce. When the silk worm is fully grown, six of them will make an ounce Thus in a few weeks these insects are multiplied in weight and hulk nine hundred fold.

From the Barbadian, April 4 1838. Vessels from St. Lucia have brought several gentlemen we understand from that Island, as a deputation from the Bar, to his Excellency the Governor-General, that Island having been lately included by her Majesty in the Government of the Windward Islands, his Excellency teceiving an additional salary of £500 sterling per annum. The object of the deputation is reported to be, to obtain from the Governor General a reversal of the Proclamation lately issued by Colonel Bunbury, which prohibits the use of the French language under certain circumstances in the Royal Court. It is also reported, (for we have no St. Lucia papers by these vessels, nor have had any for some time past), that the Chipf Justice Dr. IIeddie lately suspended by Col. Bunbury, has been reinstated by order from the Colonial Office ; and that the Chief Justice, on being replaced in judicial authority, has released the second Puisne Judge, Mr. Lafitte, from the þÿ durance þÿvile. in which the arbitrary Colonel had lately placed the hon gentleman. The prediction of the gentleman who communicated to us two months ago the particulars of that dark transaction, would appear, therefore, to have been very quickly verified. þÿ But, (said he) the avenger is behind þÿ tho' distant, yet certain, þÿ and omnipotent to do justice I for it is a British Queen , and a British people þÿ! pro bably he did not anticipate, that a British Colonial Secretary of State would be so prompt to render justice.

Sugar from Indian Corn. þÿ M Pallas lately presented to the Academic des Sciences of Paris, sample a of this substance extracted from the stem of the plant, which has been found to contain nearly six per cent, of syrup boiled to 40 degrees, a part of which will not crystallize before fructification : but it condenses and acquires more consistency from that period to the state of complete maturity. The most favourable time to obtain the greatest quantity of sugar is immediately after the maturity and gathering of the fruit. The latter left the extraction of the sugar is capital to feed cattle or to make packing paper. þÿ Ibid.

The Use of a Hat. þÿ It ought to be known as generally as possible, that a man's hat will serve in most cases as a temporary life-preserver to persons in hazard of drowning, by attending to the following directions : þÿ When a person finds himself in, or about to be in, the water, let him lay hold of his hat between his hands, laying the crown close under his chin, and the mouth under the water. By this means the quantity of air contained in the cavity of the hat will be sufficient to keep the head above water for several hours, or until assistance can be rendered. þÿ Ibid March 31.

Stepping into the Theatre last night, I was very much struck by the performance of the youthful Miss Monier, who gave Mr. Forrest an eliicient support in the arduous character which he personated with so much effect. þÿ But it was particularly in the afterpiece that the merits of this young lady, whom I saw for the first time, made an impression upon me. 1 hesitate not to predict that she is destined to perform a brilliant part upon the scenic boards. She has all the requisites for such distinction. A fine person, a genteel carriage, a handsome and intellectual countenance, and, above all, a happy combination of intelligence and sensibility, endow her with rare advantages for dramatic excellence. þÿ The manner in which she spoke the spirited epilogue, was alone sufficient to stamp her as a person of no ordinary talent. The unanimous satisfaction of a large and intelligent audience gives confirmation to the opinion 1 have expressed. This testimony is due to the distinguished merits of a young lady who gives such brilliant promise of future distinction. þÿ Washington (I lobe, March 17.

From the St. Thomas Times, April 11, 1838. Description of Queen Victoria by an Irishman. þÿ The following extract from the letter of an Irish Gentleman to his friend in Dublin, in which he gives a glowing description of our most Gracious Sovereign, is from the Standard: þÿ þÿ 1 have seen her Majesty ; O that you could see her likewise. She is in truth a royal dame. 1 had never seen royalty before, and the lirst view ot that fair form dazzled my vision. I was astonished that a person of such exquisite beauty should have been so ill described þÿ indeed, so comparatively little spoken of for such unrivalled charms. The English are a wonderful people, truly a noble race, but they lack much of that enthusiasm of us Irish ; it is not want of taste that has prevented them giving the world a just description of the young, graceful, and exquisitely fair sovereign, as theirs is most delicate; but it is, 1 that the English look more to mental qualifi-

nation than we do, and that a winning loveliness of form is with them a matter of but secondary consideration. Perhaps they are the more sensible, we the more ardent people. Her Majesty is not low in stature, as we in Ireland had been led to consider. She is apparently of that captivating Venus size, so highly prized and much admired in Latin and Grecian lore. Her Majesty was sitting when 1 had the high privilege of seeing her ; her forehead rested on a hand perhaps the smallest and whitest for a person of her age in the | as world, and her half bare arm rivalled the hand in symmetry and whiteness. Her dress was dark, and sufficiently low to show a neck of the most graceful form. Her face is oval, her complexion fair, her hair of that rare shade of

brown for w hich you have known some ladies so much admired. And oh, such hair! soft, fine, luxuriant, divided a da Madonna, and w'orked into a crown on the hack part of the head. Her white and ample forehead well contrasted with the rich shrine of that glossy hair. Her eyebrows, rather darker than her hair, rise in gentle arches above her ample eyes of the most dazzling brilliant brightness, indicating a disposition both playful and good; they are fringed with long dark silken eyelashes, that tend to soften the sparkle of her eyes. Her nose is gracefully formed, her lips just far enough separate to show two rows of teeth like pearls, and when her Majesty was seen to smile, those iips displayed the liveliest tint of the rose contrasting well with the delicate glow on her cheek. Her þÿMajesty s shoulders are low and well formed þÿ her waist is slender and round þÿ her feet small þÿ her ancles fine her whole person exquisitely grace- þÿ ful and dignified. In a word, neither pen nor pencil can adequately pourtrav her beauty and fine form. You must come over to London to see and judge for yourself, and 1 know you will then acknowledge that half her charms have not been told : but 1 would say that what the evening star is among planets, the diamond among rich gems, the rose among flowers, such is our lovely Queen among the gentle sex. þÿ West Indian

3BAST3X For the Long-Island Star. To the Lark. I hear a voice ascending Up to the sunny skies, And see gay spirits bending, To hear its melodies ; Burst on the startled feeling I, ike friendship to the soul, In captive fetters kneeling In darkness and in goal.

And mine amongst the number Tho' humblest of the train, Awakens from its slumber, To hear that voice again. Herald the morning's brightness, And fill the air with song, And lend its harp its lightness So long on willows hung. Thou golden breasted psalmist, Of morning's ruddy joy, Thine is the sweetest, calmest Praise, that may tongues employ, I listen to thine artles, And Heaven-directed lay, It is not like the heartless Cold gratitude we pay.

Unto the glorious Giver Of seasons warm and fair, Of mountain, and of river, And beauty, printed there ; Unto the hand that carries, The blossoms to the trees, And sends ten thousand glories On every genial breeze.

I greet thee, lovely charmer, 1 welcome thee once more, My friendship waxeth warmer To see thee upward soar ; So gay and so resplendent, Upon thy spotted wing þÿ I'll be thy glad attendant Sweet harbengor of Spring. Oysterponds, March 10, 1838. I. 0. T.
