From the Barbadian, March HI, 1838. KING LOUIS PHILIPPE EN KOBE DE CHAMBKE.

(from þÿ gazette de þÿfkanckfort. ) King Louis Philippe rises every morning nt eight þÿo clock. His first care is to read the letters which are handed him, and to dispatch the most urgent affairs. This done, he proceeds at nine þÿo clock to his dressingroom, where his family arc admitted While the Queen, the Princesses, and their brothers arc carrying on a conversation, in general gay, animated, and unreserved, the King shaves himself, and bestows the most minute and careful attention on his teeth, which arc very white and regular. Having finished his toilette, during which he never ceases to join in the conversation of his family, the King sits down among them, embraces his children, and amuses himself greatly with the sallies in

gAgtjfc TliTOijgl agWgCTgg £Tgg» which they indulge, and to which he takes a pleasure in exciting them by his own example. At ten þÿo clock the King makes a frugal breakfast This meal is of short duration ami generally composed of potatoes, dressed with great simplicity. On lising from table he generally visits the masons and builders employed about the chateau, where works & alterations are almost incessantly going on. F/om these excursions his Majesty frequently j returns with his habiliments covered with mortar and dust for he takes great pleasure in creeping under the scaffoldings and dim. bing to the roof, to assure himself that the works are executed in strict compliance with his orders. He chats with the workmen, who are seldom aware that the man with whom they converse so familiarly is no other than the King of the French. These excursions terminate at one, when

King never fails to be present at their meetings ; he sits down at the common table, takes immediate possession of a sheet of paper, and while attentively listening to their deliberation, he sketches with his pen a variety of figures either grotesque or fanciful. þÿ In these, drawings is observed a great deal of what our artists cal! chique. On the day when Aliband attempted to assasinate him | the King had drawn a group of aquatic birds, which it is said, Fielding would not have disavowed. The King closes the sitting by recapitulating the arguments that have been ) the day to disturb his good humour, iiis Maused, and almost always points out the course to be pursued. The Council having been broken up, he takes leave of his Ministers and retires, The latter then dispute with one another the possession of the sketches that have escaped from the lloyal pen. These sketches afterwards serve to enrich the albums of the ladies about the Court, while the artist himself, probably, little dreams of the value attached to his performances. The King next wanders through the Tuilerics and Louvre. He is at present much occupied with the galleries preparing for the Spanish Museum, which is to be placed in the wing where the clock is, and in that opposite to the Font des Arts. As an ante-chamber to these galleries there will be a room fitted up with a variety of articles belonging to the time of Henry 1 þÿV whieh have been found in the Tuileries, for Louis Philippe professes a

most enthusiastic veneration for the Bearnais. The King often enters the ateliers of the numerous artists employed about the' Louvre. þÿ The painters to whom he appeals most particularly are Messrs. Alau and Court. The King sits down with them, examines their designs with the eye of a connoisseur, pronounces his opinions, which are almost dictated by sound criticism, and takes evident delight in seeing their pictures terminated. þÿ takes notes of every thing, and classifies When he leaves these ateliers helms been noticed to sigh, and cast a melancholy look on the Place de Louvre and the quays, recollecting with the regret the time when, with his umbrella under his arm, he wandered Unaccompanied through the streets of Paris, visiting the buildings in a state of progress and almost invariably stopping before the þÿ hops of the dealers in prints and Ethographs. About two years ago an officer of his household attempted to reprimand a captain of the National Guard, who came all bespattered with mud to take his place at the royal table þÿ þÿ Blame him þÿnot, said the King, þÿ he's a

happy fellow to have it in his power to make himself þÿdirty. (It est bien heurevx depauvoir se crotter ainsi.) At dinner the Queen sits down with her children, her sister in-law, and the guests who have been invited, without waiting for the King, who seldom arrives till towards the end of the repast He helps himself to a plate of soup, whieh he frequently sends away after tasting it, on finding that it is got cold. A fowl boiled with rice (poulet a u riz, )is then placed before him ; this fie cuts up with his own hand, and generally eats nearly the whole of it. He then takes up a bunch of grapes or a handful of dry fruit, rises from table, and with his desert in his tiand withdraws to an adjoining apartment, where all the newspapers published in France are laid out for his perusal. The King very attentively peruses this mass of political dissertations, and seems to the Council of Ministers assembles. The | find much amusement in the irreverent jests at his expense, in which the pettis journaux 1 so unsparingly abound. At the time when the Chartvari and the Caricature published nearly every day a grotesque representation of the royal person, he was often seen to laugh heartily at their sketches, and in the evening talked of them in his family service, at times even showing them about with his own hand After he has read the papers the King joins the Queen in her salon, and receives the persons admitted to the evening reception. If nothing has happened during

jesty's conversation is unreserved and highly instruclive. He has seen much, is extremely well informed, tells a story remarkably well, and takes evident pleasure in doing so. If any foreigner of distinction happens to be admitted to the circle, the King, who speaks several languages with great facility, usually addresses him in his native tongue, and the manner with which he does this is calculated to gain the hearts even of those least disposed to be favourable to him Louis Philippe, it must not be forgotten, is a man of the most strict morality. Never has he afforded an opportunity to the most audacious calumny to breathe even an indirect insinuation against his private life. He is kind and full of amenity to all who are employed in his service, but he is strict in exacting from them the most punctual performance of their several duties. The most perfect order and cleanliness must prevail everywhere around him, and any infringement on these rules is sure to draw down upon the offender a reproof, not the less painlul fur being pronounced with temperance. Afterwards the King retires to his own apartment, undresses, puts on his dressing gown, and often works till two or three in the morning He never, by any chance, affixes his signature to any document, without having first ascertained the nature of its contents. He these notes according to a method of his own, intending to facilitate future reference. To every sentence of death the King devotes a most religious attention ; every document

connected with the trial must be submitted to him, he studies them in a most conscientious manner and never signs them till tie has acquired a perfect conviction of tiie guilt of the assassin. If his work is finished at an early hour, the King repairs to þÿ the Qucen'9 apartment: if not, a lit dr champ is repaired for him, the hardness of which must remind the royal sleeper of the couch of the professor of Ueicheiiau.

OPENING OF THE STATES OF HANOVER. (From the Hanover Gazette.) On the 20th instant. King Ernest opened in person the session of the States of Hanover. After the celebration of Divine Service in the Castle Chape), the members of the States repaired to the hall of the legislative body and took the oath tendered to them by the hereditary marshal of the kingdom, Count Monster. The Prince Royal also attended at this ceremony. At a quarter past two o'clock the Royal cortege left the Castle, and on reaching the Legislative Palace his Majesty was received bv the hereditary marshal and (he members of the boards of both houses. 1 he King having then entered the hall, seated himself on his throne, the Prince Royal being on his right, and the grand dignitaries of the crown on his left, and delivered the following speech : þÿ " Noble Lords, worthy and faithful Deputies, þÿ My anxious desire to see assembled round my throne the worthy states of this kingdom is at length gratified. It is tor me a great satisfaction. V\ him 1 determined on abrogating the fundamental law of December 20, 1833, by the promulgation ot my royal patents of November 1, 1837, an attempt w as made to create a belief that it was mv intention to arrogate to myself an arbitrary power over the subjects Providence has committed to my care. I have ever detested an arbitrary form of government, and I wish to govern mv beloved people only according to law and justice. In order, worthy Slates, to give you an unquestionable proof of the uprightness of

my intentions, I will shortly cause to be laid before you the draught of a new constitution fir mv kingdom, based on the principles which have so long secured the prosperity ol the people of Germany. I indulge the hope that my views will perfectly coincide with yours on all the main points of the new charter. Various other important bills will also be submitted to your deliberation. 1 declare that the Session of the States is opened." After delivering this Speech, the King left the hall to return to his palace. The royal cortege followed the same order as on its way to the house, and his Majesty received on his passage through the streets as well as on his arrival before the palace, unequivocal proofs of the satisfaction and affection ot his subjects. At five o'clock there was a grand dinner at the Castle, to which the members of both houses were invited. Immediately after the King had retired, the members of the First Chamber of the States repaired to the hall of their meetings to name the candidates for the Presidency. The following were elected : Messrs. þÿ Oberschenck, Count Platen llallermund, Counts Junh and Knyphausen, and de Wense. The list of candidates having been submitted to the King, his Majesty appointed President Count Platen liallermund, who immediately took the oath of office. E. lor the last twenty four hours along this coast, and although partially subsided, still blows a gale, has left behind it tokens of its visitation in the wreck ot her Majesty's packet Ranger, which packet broke from her moorins at five o'clock, a. m., from which period, for three hours> guns were continually fired by her. I he constant fall of hail and snow prevented its beinff o known on shore what position the ves- 1 sel was in, from which the reports were heard as signals for assistance. On the weather becoming a little clear she was discovered to be the packet above-mentioned, and an express soon after arrived at Captain Plutnridge's to report the event. The sea had driven her broadside on the shore, under '1 relusishtll, on the spot where the Queen, transport was lost some years ago In a short space ot time the coast was lined with sailors belonging to the packets, with their officers, and the gallant Commodore ot the port, who had hastened round to the point, about four miles distant from Falmouth by land, and were engaged iu saving her stores, Ac. It is to be hoped that she will yet be able to get oil on the next spring tides, if the continuance ot the recent gales does not shatter her frame. A man, called Andrews, was drowned. An instance of great intrepidity occurred today. When the wind was at its height,

two men were seen on board a coal finikin the harbour exerting themselves to the utmost in pumping her, and likewise a coal bag hoisted to a spar, indicating distress. It being known that the hulk was leaky, the circumstance was talked of amongst the crowd of persons who were looking on as one of the greatest perils, and unless the men were uken otr immediately, that they would perish. At tins moment, Lieutenant Field. R N. happened to be passing, and on his hearing the circumstance, hastened to the pier, and engaged a six-oared longboat to attempt to rescue the poor fellows from destruction : the gallant officer not only bribed the boatmen with his pocket, but likewise shared their danger, and after very great exertion they happily succeeded in liberating the men from, to all appearance, a watery grave. Lieutenant Field is in command ol the Rapid, the South Australian Commissioners' brig, awaiting dispatches in this harbour. It is to be hoped that this meritorious noble act will meet with the reward it deserves from the government. þÿ llnd.

Elegant Compliment þÿ There scarcely ever was a finer compliment paid to a lady, than that which Dean Swift addressed to a wife, who was always praising her husband : " You always are making a god of your spouse, But that neither reason nor conscience allows. Perhaps you think 'lis ingratitude due And you adore him berause he adores you, Your argument's weak and so will you find, For you by this rule, must adore all mankind."

We extract for the information of our readers, the following brief sketch of the general plan proposed to be adopted by Mr. M'Queen, in carrying into effect the conveyance of mails by steam between Great Britain and the Western World. The Guiana Chronicle on this topic thus pays its tribute of praise to the talented author of this plan. " Mr. M'Queen is now fast sinking into the vale ot years, and consequently proportionably withdrawing lrom public life, of which he was so long an ornament, into the calmer scenes ot private retirement : it is therefore possible that the formation of this beneficial and highly practicable plan may be the last effort of his devotion and service to the cause of the West Indians. Should it be so þÿ which we sincerely hope may not be the case þÿ the closing act of his public career will indeed be worthy of his earlier course þÿ it will be, in short, adding the capita! to the pillar of his already well won fame a fame, not bolster- þÿ ed up by acts as specious as they are inutile, but based upon the services of years of his efficient and unwearted advocacy of the cause of his adoption þÿ the welfare and interests of the calumniated and misrepresented West Indians.

The route of this Boat would be. Barbados to Laguayra, calling first at St. Vincent's and Grenada, 510 miles, 4 days; stop there 4 days and to Nt. Thomas, 400 miles, 5 days : to Barbados, 8 days; in all 21 days. Two Schooners would do this work, giving two mails each month.

On the arrival of the British Packet at Barbados a fast sailing schooner should be dispatched, as at present, with the outward mails from Great Britain for St. Lucia, Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe, Antigua, Montserrat, Nevis and St. Kitt's. The boat need proceed no further westward than St Kitt's, because the boat from Barbados had carried forward the Tortola mails. From St. Kitt's it will return to Barbados, calling at all the Islands just enumerated, for the return Colonial mails. The route of this boat would be, Barbados to St. Kitts, calling at the places mentioned, 370 miles, 4 days ; and baclv to Baibados, b days ; together ten days. " On the eight day after the arrival of the Packet at Barbados (the dispatch of this boat must always be so as to secure its arrival at St. Kitt's before the Packet,) a schooner to be dispatched with the return mails and passengers from that island, to pick up for the homeward bound Packet mails and passengers at St. Lucia, Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe, Antigua, Montserrat, and Nevis, and give or to leave these for the Packet at St. Kitt's, From St. Kitts this boat returns to Barbados, calling at all the islands enumerated for the return Colonial mails. This boat will be the same time out as the one which carried the outward mails, namely, ten days. " Two schooners will do the work on both the course here pointed out as necessary, with two spare ones at Barbados, in case of the arrival of the Packets on the heels of each other

from Britain, to forward the mails for all the places mentioned and for Laguayra, making in all eight schooners for this station. There are at present ten or more. Catharine IMc'Innes. or the wrong letter ii"x. Amusing incidents often occur by persons mistaking the letter box of stores and offices in this vicinity, for that of the Post Office. þÿ We sometimes find three or four letters in our own letter box, intended for the mails. þÿ These we, of course, put on their way. Standing once at our front window, we observed a young woman, whose face was not visible to us, drop a letter into our box, and on taking it out, we found that she had mistaken our establishment for that of the Post Office. It was directed to Thomas , in Ireland, and the inland postage accompanied it. The letter we caused to be sent with some others to the Post Office, and gave the circumstance no farther thought. Busied a few months afterward in examining the contents of our exchange papers, and inditing such paragraphs as they suggested to us, we did not pay much attention to a gentle tap at the door of our private room, until it was repeated. We then, too anxious to conclude our labors to open to the applicant, bade the one that knocked " come in," and continued our labors without lifting an eye to the door, which was opened quietly, and as quietly closed. We were startled at length with a sweetly modulated voice, inquiring " is there a letter here for tnc ?" We at once raised our eves, and saw a female about eighteen years of age þÿ or, as

©AW3BL T33T3»»33"r ®'J8B3a'J83Sr®3 AT33 we have of late lost the art of judging closely in these matters, perhaps twenty. It did not make a dimple's difference to her face, and would not if five more years had been added to them. There was an oval face, þÿ with nature's own blush, and a slight projection of the mouth ihat told of Ireland, even without the softened modulation of voice that belongs to the women of that Island. Neatness was all that could be ascribed to her dress þÿ ii deserved that. Letters are frequently asked for in a newspaper office, in reply to þÿadvertisements so we bade the young woman go to the front office and inquire of the clerks. She had been there, and there was no one but a boy, who could not give her the information. So we inquired the name. " Kitty Mcinnes ; but perhaps it will be Catharine on the letter," said she, " as that is my name." We looked on the letter rack in the front office, among the A. B.'s" the X. W.'s," " " the " P Q.'s," &c. but saw none for Catharine. Returning, we inquired to what advertisement the letter was to be an answer. "Advertisement! to no advertisement þÿ þÿ it would be in answer to my letter." " And from whom did you expect a letter ' The young woman looked much confused þÿ but apparently supposeing the question pertinent, she said, from Thomas We saw at once tiiat she had, as hundreds before had done, mistaken our office for the Post Office, and the name given was that upon the letter which we had some months before sent from our letter box to tiiat of the

l'ost Office. " He has not written, then," said Catharine, in a low voice, evidently not intended for our ear. " l!ui he may have written." " Then whore's the letter !" said she, looking up. " A; the Post Office, perhaps." And we took Catharine by the hand and led her to the door, and pointed out the way to the Post Office " You will ask at the window," said we ; " but as the clerks are young men, you need not tell them from whom you expect the letter." " Not for the world," said she, looking into our face with a glance that seemed to say tiiere was no harm in telling us. We must have used less than our usual precision in directing Catharine to the Post Office, as quite half an hour afterward, when visiting the place, we saw her at the window, receiving the change and a letter from one of the clerks, and the impatience, shall we say of woman or of love, induced Catharine to break the seal at the door. A glow of pleasure was on the check of the happy girl. We would not have given a penny to be informed that Thomas was well, ' and was coming o in the next packet. We felt anxious to know whether Thomas would come, but the name ol such persons rarely appear among the passengers of the Liverpool packet, being commonly included in that comprehen ive line, " and two hundred in the steerage." So we gave up all hopes of knowing when Thomas would arrive, but concluded that we would see the name with that of Catharine in the marriage list, to which we had determined to keep a steady look.

It was but a short time nfWwnrd that we did indeed see the name of Thomas in the papers He was one of the passengers in the ship cast away below New York, of whom nearly every soul perished, and Thomas among the rest. We had never seen Thomas, but had somehow cherished such an interest in his fate, that we felt a severe shock at its annuncin lion þÿ and what must have been the feelings of Catharine, with her ardent, sanguine, Irish temperament Loving deeply as she must have loved, and hoping ardently as she must have hoped, what must have been her feelings ? We paused a few weeks afterward, to mark the young grass shooting, green and thick, in Ronaldson's grave yard, and to see the buds swelling on the branches of the trees that decorate that populous city of the dead, when a funeral, numerously attended, wound slowly round the corner of the street, and passed into the enclosure. It was the funeral of an Irish person þÿ we knew by the numbers that attended þÿ and as the sexton lowered the coffin down into the narrow house, the place appointed for all the living, we saw engraved upon a simple plate. Catharine Mc'Innes. The story was told. The small sum of money which Catharine had deposited in the saving fund to give a little consequence to her marriage festival, had been withdrawn to give her " decent burial."

The Faubourg St. Honore has just been the theatre of a tragic scene. M ine. I , , when very young, was the constant playmate of a youth named B . Their juvenile friendship, in course of years grew into a warmer attachment. At the age of 21, II was obliged to go into the countrv for several months. On his return, he found that Ins fair friend had been induced to marry another. Their intimacy was renewed, and their former passion revived. A lengthened absence of the husband unfortunately a th Tiled a too favorable opportunity for its guiliv indulgence. þÿ At last M. h. announced by letter bis approaching return. This threw the lovers into despair, and they resolved not to be separated but bv death. þÿ Having sent away all the househould, they on Mondav last, shut themselves up. and having procured and lighted several charcoal braziers, accomplished their purpose by suffocation. (In Tuesday morning the husband returned found the outer-door double locked within, and perceived a mephitic odour issuing from the apartment. Having forced an enlrancc, he found the dead body of young B. on the lied, and the wife lying by his side, in the last agonies, with her arm round his neck. She had just strength enough left to open her eves upon her injured husband, and then expired. þÿ Paris Paper.

MONEY MARKET. Cirv, Wednesday Evening, Apmo 11. The question of resumption by our Banks is hastening to a close. It has been moote d long enough in all conscience. The convention now in session can do no more than carry out the predetermination of our Banks. For any good that its assemblage can effect, it might as well have not taken place In the treatment of this whole subject of resumption, there has been a sort of betise distinguishing the conduct of our great financiers, quite impossible to account for. That any man in his senses could have for a moment supposed, the General Government would favor the resuming Banks, is an inexplicable phenomenon. Yet there are men in this city, good and staunch Whigs, and papers too of the same faith, that express a belief, Mr. Van Buren will not oppress the resuming Banks. There is no accounting for the vagaries of some men's minds. But we will be charitable, and refer such a strange profession of political faith to the instigations of their private interests, that prevent the judgment from arriving at the truth. The unanswerable letter of Mr. Biddle seems to have kindled anew the ire of these new doctrinaires, and they vie with the Loco Focos in abuse of the eminent writer. Indeed the Evening Post is far more honorable in its review of this letter, than our dissenting friends. Mr. Biddle is not a mere financier, but he views the subject before him with all the calmness of a statesman, a philosopher, and a political economist. Our Banks will i fond of

find to their sorrow that nothing will ever place the banking and credit system on its feet again, short of the expulsion of the Vandals from the high places they now occupy. Ere 1840, Mr. Riddle's letter will have proved prophetic. Every man of cool judgment must assent to its truth. A large sale of stocks took place to day, mostly of the fancies. We regret to see that U. S. Bank left ofl at 1 1 1 ) This is fait part . of the workings of the new elements against this bank. Yesterday at Philadelphia, the stock of this institution sold at 1 17 J Specie is almost at par with New York notes. þÿ Treasury notes continue at their old rates þÿ from ; to 3 per cent discount.

A Fight with the Devil. þÿ The events of the following narrative took place some years since, in the town of Columbia, Fluvanna county, Virginia, where I first set out in life, and opened a grocery ; and to my shamerl say it, 1 soon became to do like the best part of all who deal in ardent spirits ; þÿ 1 at first despised even the taste of it, but soon become to like it loo well for my good. 1 bought a lot in that place of one Peyton, who was very goats ; and when he moved into the country, he left a young kid with me, which the boys about town learned to butt, by getting on all fours, while it was young. It never forgot this practise after it was grown up He was black, and had a large pair of horns. About the time I first opened my grocery, there was a certain T. C , in the full glee of drinking. He was a large man, was said to be the champion of the country, and had a large face. Soon after what I am going to relate, he went the way of all drunkards to an untimely grave. He þÿ left town one night, where he had been drunk nearly day all ; and when be started, he was very much intoxicated, and bought a bottle of spirits of me. Some time in the night, (the moon shone bright,) some persons knocked at my door. 1 got up and opened it ; and who should it be, but T. C. His face was very bloody, and there were great knots on it nearly as largo as hen's eggs. I asked him what was the matter; what had happened I He said that he had a fight with the devil. þÿ

He said he was black, and had a large pair of horns I asked him if he thought he could show me the battle ground ? He said yes. The next morning he carried me to the old field where the goat used to stay, and tficre were the tracks of the goat, where he had torn up the ground by mnking foul charges against his head This I certify to be true. þÿ WILLIAM WEAVER.

þÿIWMl I III Mil 'tTTini There has lately been discovered in England a mode of warming an apartment by placing in the midst of it a portable vase, which emits neither flame or smoke, and which will raise the temperature of the air in a room of any dimensions to the degree required. The vase is called the Portable Warming Apparatus You may, says an English journal, set it on a table or take it in a carriage, and it will warm a public hail, or a pew in a church What the invention consists of is not yet known ; nor will it be made public till patents are secured for other parts of the world besides England. it is some chemical combination producing combustion without flame, and generating heat that radiates with such velocity as to warm every part of the surrounding atmosphere almost simultaneously, without raising the h u:p, mature of the metal containing it to such a degree as to scorch any thing coming in contact. Its consumption of the oxygen of the am is said to be so small that a vase sufficient to warm a large room does not consume more than a rushlight would, and its expense is almost as trivial, being only three pence sterling for twenty-four hours. A carriage or closet might be warmed for fifteen hours at the rate of one penny. This discovery it is said was accidently made by a market gaidener while opening a hot bed. Such is the account which is given of this wonderful invention. The London Spectator falls into a pleasant speculation on the changes which it will effect in the þÿworld.

The " Englishman's fireside," of which there is so much talk, will be abolished ; stoves will be seen only in kitchens, for this new heat will not answer for culinary purposes ; the iron mongers will vend no more parlor grates ; the canopy of smoke will be lifted from London ; the chimneys will be levelled to the roofs; London will breathe a new atmosphere and wear a new aspect ; the occupation of the sweeps will be gone, except when they are called to sweep the kitchen flue, and the alarm which many have f> It lest the supply of coals should fail will Ire quieted for ever. þÿ N Y. StARSR /or <Ae Long-Island Star. . THE MOTHER'S HI Ell. Stately and tall, they gather round þÿ Sons, round a mother's bier ; And youth, and health, and strength are theirs; What means that woman-tear?
Had strength availed þÿ could love have saved The dear one by their side, Or manly hearts her danger braved, " Their mother had not died."
Still, still on earth, the wearied dove Had sought a place of rest ; Untasted still the joys above þÿ The raptures of the blest.
But, joy ! it was her Savior's call And angel- wings were given ; Vainly would earthly ties enthrall þÿ Her destined home was Heaven !
Yet weep, weep on ! let burning tears Flow fast, arm full, and free ! Such love as blessed your early years, Ye ne'er again shall see !
W ecp on ! the mothers voice, is hushed, That would have soothed that grief; Forever gone the mother's love, That ever brought relief.
Weep on, weep on ! for tears may soothe, If not assuage your pain ; Yet joy ! for yrour time-bounded loss, Is her eternal gain ! S. Brooklyn, March 15, 1838.

Steam Frigate Fulton. A Correspondent of the Baltimore Patriot, writing from New York, thus describes this floating steam battery : "The courtesy of Copt. Perry, TJ. S. N, brother to the immortal hero of same name, enabled me by a short cruise in the frigate Fulton, on Thursday, to appreciate the value of a steam battery. One thousand tons burthen, propelled by engines capable of exerting nine hundred horse power, moving at the rate of 13 knots an hour, presenting a small surface above water to hostile cannon, armed with six 68 pounders, and enabled by the distance at which she can hull an enemy, without exposure to a return fire, she is invaluable in harbor defence and if the system is carried out will render useless further expenditures 011 fortifications. Her engines are perfect þÿ no vibratory jar from the immense propelling force, and a child with his feeble arm turned a crank, which, in an instant arrested the progress of tins moving Leviathan, and brought her to repose in perfect stillness.

Spaix vxd hi:k affairs. Our last account from Spain, represents the Civil War as yet raging, although with diminished violence. Spain, as is well known to our readers, is divided into two parties, the Queen's party and the Carlist's. Their origin is as follows. Ferdinand VII, the late King of Spain married in his old age a young wife, the daughter of the King of Naples. She of course had her lover, Munaor bv name, a handsome and gallant Spanish cavalier. Before the death of Ferdinand, a daughter was born to the royal pair, and being an only child, the Salique law which prohibits the succession of females to the throne was repealed, thus excluding the claims of Don Carlos, the eldest brother of the king. Cpon the death of Ferdinand therefore, the whole kingdom arose in arms ; the liberal party siding with the Infanta and the Queen Regent : the priests and the old Christians as they called themselves, with Don Carlos. Engagements took place, and hi any severe battles were fought on both sides, with victory alternating to either party, until at last tin; cause -of the Queen seems the strongest & the most popular. There is one circumstance however, which prejudices the moral

&n<MSSUIir<lft8 A'ras. and religious portion of Spain against the Queen Regent, and that is the fact of the birth of two children since she became a widow, a fact which causes many to doubt the legitimacy of the infant Queen, although born during the life time of Ferdinand. Such is a brief sketch of the dissensions which agitated this unhappy and degraded land, and which call laudly for the interference of the other powers of Europe 10 prevent its utter ruin.

The second May packet arrived since our last brings London dates ol the 15th, but tli»,y furnish little news. A great dinner was given to Sir Robert Peel by the conservative members of the House of Commons, of whom 313 subscribed, and 303 actually attended the dinner. Sir Robert made a long and eloquent speech, which was received with great enthusiasm, and he appears confident of again coming into power. The Queen had given her first hall at the new palace, Buckingham house ; about 000 with Her Majesty opened the ball attended ; Prince George of Cambridge, as her partner. A succession of Royal parties and balls are to follow the coronation. A splendid mansion has been taken for Prince Alexander of Russia, who is to remain, it is said, two months in London A grand review by Her Majesty of all the household troops in London was to take place the anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo; it is supposed that all the foreign princes who are to visit England at the coronation, will be present. Espartero had gained a victory over Negri, Don Carlos general, and captured 2,000 prisoners. A motion has been made in the House of Commons to rescind the resolution of April 1835, relative to the Irish church. The success of that motion caused the resignation of Sir Robert Peel in 1835. The conservatives think they can now carry the motion to rescind, which may lead to a change of ministry. It was to be taken up in a few days.
A motion to allow foreign Corn to he in England into flour, and sold for exportation, has been rejected in the House of Commons, ayes 150 noes 220

Franklin, Miss. April 10. A planter of this parish has just returned tiom N. Orleans, who sold his crop of sugar at Mobile, which brought him in that market $0000. To get $0000 from Mobile to New Orleans, a distance of about 150 miles, and which a good steamboat accomplishes in about fourteen hours, this planter has actually paid 17 percent, amounting to the sum of $1,020. What sav our cane growers to such an exchange as that ? Did they ever hear of such a thing till our wise administration began to þÿ improve the þÿcurrency? þÿ When the L nited States Bank had branches in the south, this planter might have taken the bills which he received at Mobile, to the counter of the branch, and exchanged it at par for bills of the United States Bank, and these were current in any part of the Union. He could pay his debts with these in St. Marv, or he could travel to New York or Boston with them, and pay his debts there. But now he has paid out of one sixth part of a

portion of his property, to get it in such money as he could pay his debts within Louisiana. And the effect of the experiment on the remainder of his property is as great as it is on this. What say our planters to this sacrifice of one-sixth of their property in an þÿ þÿexperiment. And we ask þÿagain did they Aver know any thing of this kind while the United States Bank had branches in all parts of the country ? Never.

In an introductory lecture of great splendour and eloquence, delivered some time ago by the illustrious l)r Chalmers, he made the following vigorous and judicious remarks in relation to the liberties that had been taken with theology by certain daring scientific speculators : þÿ At one period arose geology from the earth's depths and entered into mortal combat with a revelation which, pillared on the evidence of history, withstood the assault At another from the attitudes of the upper firmament was astronomy brought down, and arrayed in hostile attitude against the records of our faith; and this attack has also proved powerless as the former. þÿ Then, from themvsteries of the human spirit, an attempt lias been industriously made to induce some discovery of wondrous spell, by which to disenchant the world of its confidence in the Gospel of Jesus Christ. þÿ From lecture rooms of anatomy, both in London and elsewhere, the lessons of materialism have been inculcated, and that for the purpose of putting a mockery on all religion, and driving it, if possible, from the face of the earth. þÿ Hut the most singular attempt to graft infidelity on any thing purporting to be a science has been made by those who associate the doctrines of phrenology with their denial of the Christian revelation, as it there were any earthly connexion between the form of the human skull and the truth or falsehood of our religion. The science of theology lias

been made a sort of play-ground foi all manner of inreads in regard to human speculation; but it is not without a peculiar evidenced its own. unassailable and beyond the reach of external violence. It is not the hammer of the mineralogist that can break this evidence. It is not the telescope of the astronomer that can enable us to descry in it any character of falsehood. It is not bv the knite of the anatomist. that vve can find our wa\ to the alleged rottenness which lies at its core It is not by dissecting metaphysics that the mental of philosopher can probe bis way to the secret of its insufficiency, and make exposure to the world of the yet unknown flaw v hit h vitiates the proofs of the Christian faith. At 'hose sciences have at one time or other, c.as' their missiles at the stately fabric of our Christian philosophy and erudition þÿ but they have iropt harmless and impotent at its þÿbase þÿ The entire scope and strain of this lecture was not to throw any discredit on the sound and legitimate achievement of science ; but to visit with merited censure and reprobation those crude visionary theories which have for their dangerous object the dissemination of infidel principles.
